replies.text:
Step 2 checks:

- Automated abuse of reachable entry points: design has it — "Customers open support tickets on our website and can attach any file." Covered by listed threat 5 (anonymous bot flood of intake/attachments).
- Staff screens rendering user-supplied content: design has it — "Support agents open the attachments in the agent console, which runs in their browser" — covered by listed threat 3 (script in privileged agent session).
- Privileged actions with no record of who did it: design has the access but no accountability — "the agent console, which runs in their browser with access to every customer record"; listed threat 2 covers the exposure breadth, not the absence of any record of which agent read/exported which customer. Not covered.
- Personal documents cacheable by browsers/proxies/CDNs: design has "Attachments are stored in a public-read storage bucket so the console can link to them directly" — this is a sub-case of listed threat 1 (public URL readable by anyone); not a separate gap.
- Attacker-controlled text reaching logs, CSV/spreadsheet exports, emails or headers: design states no export, log, email or downstream system. Not present.
- Single-reviewer items: metadata/path trust depends on how upload is built (not stated); "links not tied to the ticket owner" is the same public-URL weakness as listed threat 1; phishing-hosting duplicates listed threat 4.

  "schema": "threatline.threatmodel.v1",
  "issueKey": "EVAL-02",

    "components": ["public ticket intake form", "agent console (browser)", "attachment storage bucket", "customer record store"],
    "dataStores": ["public-read storage bucket", "customer records"],
    "externalServices": [],
    "trustBoundaries": ["anonymous website visitor to intake", "agent console to customer record store"],
    "dataClasses": ["pii"],
    "exposure": "public",
    "llmFeatures": false
  },
  "threats": [
    {
      "stride": "Repudiation",
      "title": "No record of which agent viewed or exported which customer records",
      "scenario": "The console gives every agent browser session access to every customer record, and the design describes no logging of which agent opened or pulled which customer. An agent (or whoever hijacks an agent session) can browse or bulk-read customer records for people whose tickets they never handled, then deny it; the company cannot tell during an incident which records were actually touched or scope a breach notification. Abuse of the broad access stays invisible instead of being detected.",
      "component": "agent console access to customer records",
      "likelihood": 4,
      "impact": 3,
      "rating": { "attacker": "insider", "effort": "low", "reach": "all", "harm": "minor" },
      "evidence": [
        { "quote": "Support agents open the attachments in the agent console, which runs in their browser with access to every customer record." }
      ],
      "asvs": ["V7.1.3"],
      "cwe": ["CWE-778"],
      "plainLanguage": "Agents can look at any customer's record and nothing writes down who looked at what, so misuse can't be proven or even spotted.",
      "requirement": {
        "title": "Log every agent access to customer records and attachments",
        "given": "an agent session in the support console that can reach every customer record",
        "when": "the agent views, searches or exports a customer record or opens an attachment",
        "then": "the system writes a tamper-resistant audit entry with agent identity, customer/ticket identifier, action and timestamp, retained for review and alerting on bulk access"
      }
    }
  ]
}
